common_name: Metechi Hardneck Garlic (Republic of Georgia Rocambole Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, several weeks before the ground freezes, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil; Metechi is a Rocambole type and needs a real winter chill to size up properly, so it performs best where winters are reliably cold.

directions: Plant cloves pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Metechi is a Rocambole-type hardneck heirloom brought out of the Republic of Georgia, grown for its rich, robust, full-bodied garlic flavor and large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single ring around a hard central stalk. Like other Rocamboles it sends up a distinctive coiling scape in early summer, which should be cut once it curls to redirect the plant's energy into bulb size, and the bulbs store only moderately well compared to porcelain or silverskin types, so plan to use this variety earlier in the storage season. It demands a genuine cold winter to break dormancy and form full-sized bulbs, making it best suited to northern and mountain gardens rather than the Deep South.

common_name: Georgian Fire Hardneck Garlic (Spicy Porcelain Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, in loose, well-drained, fertile soil; Georgian Fire is a vigorous porcelain type that tolerates cold winters well and stores longer than most Rocambole garlics.

directions: Plant cloves pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Georgian Fire is a porcelain-type hardneck heirloom, also brought out of the Republic of Georgia, producing large bulbs with just four to six plump, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white wrappers, and it is prized among heirloom garlic growers for a noticeably hotter, more pungent bite than milder porcelain varieties like Georgian Crystal or Music. Cut the curling scapes in early summer once they appear to push more energy into bulb development, and cure harvested bulbs in a warm, dry, airy spot for several weeks before trimming and storing. Porcelain types store considerably longer than Rocamboles, generally holding good quality for six months or more under cool, dry conditions.
